hero.headline: Trump administration imposes tariffs on 59 countries over forced labor concerns
hero.body:
The Trump administration announced tariffs ranging from 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 trading partners, including the United Kingdom, European Union, Canada, Taiwan and Australia, citing failures to adequately address forced labor in their supply chains. The move represents a strategic shift in how the administration justifies its trade policies following a major legal setback.

The Supreme Court struck down many of the administration's previous tariffs in February, ruling that the president lacked legal authority to impose them under a 1977 emergency statute. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, joined by two Trump appointees, Justices Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett. The three remaining conservative justices dissented.

By anchoring the new tariffs to forced labor concerns rather than emergency powers, administration officials believe they have found a more legally durable approach. Legal experts suggest this rationale may withstand court challenges better than the previous statutory basis, though critics argue the forced labor justification serves as cover for protectionist policies rather than a genuine human rights initiative.

The proposed tariffs immediately drew pushback from trading partners. The European Union said it expected the United States to honor a tariff agreement reached in July and argued that these new duties breach the spirit of that accord. Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva expressed indignation over separate 25 percent tariff proposals, claiming the administration was influenced by political opponents ahead of Brazil's elections.

The announcement comes as the administration manages the fallout from the Supreme Court ruling. Officials launched a digital claims system called Cape on Monday to process refunds for more than $166 billion in tariffs that were declared illegal. Customs officials acknowledged in court filings that they had to build an entirely new processing infrastructure from scratch, initially lacking even the basic capability to deposit money directly into most importers' accounts.

More than 3,000 companies have sued to secure their refunds, including high-profile businesses like Skechers, Revlon, Toyota, Nintendo of America, FedEx and Costco. Only companies that officially paid the tariffs, primarily importers and large corporations, are legally eligible to claim refunds. Ordinary consumers who absorbed costs through higher prices on electronics, clothing and other goods have no direct recourse.

The refund system will initially process claims only for entries that are unliquidated or liquidated within the past 80 days. Businesses whose goods are tied up in legal disputes or anti-dumping investigations cannot claim yet. Companies can expect to wait 60 to 90 days from submission to receive their money.

Whether consumers see any benefit depends on individual businesses. FedEx has committed to passing refunds to customers, while Costco suggested it could lower prices, though some shoppers are already suing the retailer over whether price reductions will actually materialize.

cards.headline: Iranian Drone Attack Kills One at Kuwait Airport, Dozens Injured
cards.body:
An Iranian drone attack on Kuwait's international airport killed one person and injured dozens on Wednesday, marking one of the largest assaults on a Gulf nation since a cease-fire between the United States and Iran was announced in April. Video footage verified by The New York Times showed fire inside the airport following the attack.

The strike represents a significant test of the fragile cease-fire agreement that halted direct hostilities between American and Iranian forces two months ago. Kuwait, a small Gulf state that borders Iraq to the north and Saudi Arabia to the south, hosts several American military installations and has historically maintained careful diplomatic relations with both Western powers and its larger neighbors.

The attack involved a barrage of drones targeting the airport, one of the region's busiest transit hubs. Kuwaiti authorities confirmed the death toll and said dozens of people required medical treatment for injuries sustained in the assault. The airport serves as a major connection point for travelers between Europe, Asia, and other parts of the Middle East.

Iran has not issued an official statement claiming responsibility for the attack or explaining its rationale for targeting Kuwaiti infrastructure. The timing and scale of the assault raise questions about Tehran's commitment to the April cease-fire and its broader regional strategy. Kuwait has generally avoided direct involvement in conflicts between Iran and Western-aligned nations, making the attack particularly noteworthy.

The incident adds to growing concerns about stability in the Persian Gulf region. Since the cease-fire took effect, tensions have remained high despite the formal pause in fighting between American and Iranian forces. The attack on civilian airport infrastructure marks an escalation that could prompt responses from Kuwait's allies, including the United States, which maintains a significant military presence in the country.

cards.headline: US and Iran exchange military strikes as ceasefire shows signs of strain
cards.body:
The US and Iran traded fire in what marks the most serious test yet of their month-long ceasefire agreement. Iranian forces launched multiple missiles, drones, and small boats at three American destroyers transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday evening, prompting a military response from US Central Command.

According to the US military, no American assets were damaged in the Iranian attack. US forces intercepted the incoming threats and struck back at Iranian military facilities responsible for the assault, targeting missile and drone launch sites, command centers, and surveillance operations.

Iran's military disputed the American account, accusing the US of violating the ceasefire first by targeting an Iranian oil tanker and another vessel in the strait. Iranian officials claimed the US conducted airstrikes on civilian areas along the Iranian coast, including the island of Qeshm, which is home to approximately 150,000 people and a water desalination plant. Iran's military said their forces responded by attacking US military vessels, claiming to have inflicted significant damage.

The confrontation also included attacks on Kuwait's main airport. Iran said these strikes were retaliation for earlier US military action against Iranian targets. Kuwait briefly shut its main airport after Iranian drones struck a passenger terminal.

President Donald Trump characterized the exchange as a minor incident, calling the Iranian attack a "love tap" during remarks to reporters. He said American forces "blew them away" in response and described the situation as manageable. Trump remained optimistic about diplomatic prospects, stating that a deal "might not happen, but it could happen any day" and claiming Iran wanted an agreement more than his administration did.

The military exchange comes amid stalled peace talks between the two nations. Before Thursday's fighting, reports indicated the US and Iran may have been close to a temporary agreement to halt hostilities, with a one-page memorandum being shared between Washington and Tehran through Pakistan. However, senior Iranian officials have recently rejected concessions, with some favoring extended negotiations closer to the US midterm elections in November.

The US has been pressuring Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports. Earlier in the week, the military said it had destroyed six Iranian small boats, cruise missiles, and drones while guiding stranded tankers through the waterway in an operation Trump called "Project Freedom."

Regional diplomats believe the current moment could offer an opportunity to conclude the conflict, though they also warn that Iran risks overplaying its hand. They note that if no agreement is reached, the US could unilaterally end the war, leaving Iran facing continued economic sanctions.

cards.headline: Fire at New Delhi Hotel Kills at Least 21
cards.teaser: A fire at a hotel in India's capital killed at least 21 people and injured dozens more.
cards.body:
A fire at a hotel in New Delhi killed at least 21 people and injured dozens more, according to Indian authorities. The blaze marks the deadliest fire in the Indian capital in at least four years.

Fire safety remains a persistent challenge in India, with deadly blazes occurring periodically across hotels, factories, and residential buildings throughout the country.

cards.headline: Israeli Strikes Kill Nine in Lebanon as Hezbollah Fires Rockets
cards.teaser: Israeli airstrikes killed nine people in Lebanon as Hezbollah launched rockets across the border, straining a partial cease-fire agreed two days earlier.
cards.body:
Israeli strikes killed nine people in Lebanon on Wednesday as Hezbollah fired rockets across the border into Israel. The exchange marked a significant strain on the partial cease-fire that Israel and Hezbollah had agreed to just two days earlier, with the US playing a role in brokering the deal.

Despite the violations, the truce appeared to largely hold. Israel continued its military campaign in southern Lebanon but did not strike Beirut following the agreement announced by the US.

cards.headline: Medicaid work requirements could affect people with cancer and HIV
cards.teaser: Adults on Medicaid will need to work 80 hours monthly or prove they are too sick to qualify for an exemption.
cards.body:
The Trump administration has implemented new work rules requiring adults on Medicaid to work 80 hours per month. People with serious illnesses must prove they are too sick to work in order to qualify for an exemption from these requirements.

Advocates warn that individuals with cancer or HIV could lose their Medicaid coverage under this policy. The new rules place the burden on sick individuals to demonstrate they cannot meet the monthly work threshold, potentially leaving vulnerable populations without health insurance coverage.

cards.headline: Ukraine Strikes St. Petersburg as Putin Economic Conference Opens
cards.teaser: Ukrainian drones struck targets in St. Petersburg on the first day of Russia's marquee annual economic forum.
cards.body:
Ukrainian drones struck St. Petersburg early Wednesday, targeting oil storage facilities and military sites as international guests arrived for Russia's flagship economic forum. Several long-range drones penetrated Russian air defenses, hitting an oil terminal and causing explosions with thick black smoke visible across the city.

The attack occurred hours before the opening of the annual economic conference, where President Putin is scheduled to speak on Friday. Ukrainian President Zelensky confirmed the strikes targeted a navy base and oil terminal in the region.

cards.headline: Alex Younger, Former MI6 Chief, Dies at 62
cards.teaser: The former director of Britain's foreign intelligence service led the agency from 2014 to 2020.
cards.body:
Sir Alex Younger, who led Britain's MI6 from 2014 to 2020, has died at age 62. He spent nearly three decades in British intelligence, beginning his career in 1991 before ascending to lead the espionage agency.

During his tenure as director, Younger oversaw MI6's response to major security challenges of the period, including international terrorism and Russian aggression. His leadership spanned a time of considerable geopolitical tension and evolving threats to British national security.

cards.headline: Protests Over UK Murder Case Turn Violent, 11 Officers Wounded
cards.teaser: Demonstrations over the Henry Nowak murder case turned violent, with 11 police officers injured in clashes.
cards.body:
Eleven police officers were wounded in violent clashes with demonstrators protesting the handling of the Henry Nowak murder case. Right-wing politicians and commentators have accused the police of anti-white bias in their handling of the investigation, fueling public anger.

British leaders called for calm as the protests escalated beyond peaceful demonstrations. The Nowak case has become a flashpoint for tensions over policing and allegations of unequal treatment based on race, with critics claiming authorities have applied different standards to similar cases.

cards.headline: Eight Bodies Found in Plastic Bags in Ecuador Trafficking Hotspot
cards.teaser: Authorities in Ecuador discovered eight bodies in plastic bags with a note left at the scene in an area known for narco-trafficking.
cards.body:
Eight bodies were found in plastic bags in Ecuador in an area known as a hotspot for narco-trafficking activity.

The discovery highlights ongoing violence linked to drug trafficking organizations operating in Ecuador. The country has seen an increase in violent crime related to competition among criminal groups for control of drug routes and territory.

cards.headline: Scott Pelley fired from 60 Minutes amid broader leadership shakeup
cards.teaser: The show's new leader says he fired the star correspondent for insubordination after three executives and two reporters were let go.
cards.body:
CBS fired veteran 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley this week, citing insubordination. Pelley has contested the characterization, instead accusing network executives of instructing him to "inject falsehoods and bias" into his reporting and of silencing employees.

The firing is part of a broader shake-up at the program, following the dismissal of three top executives and two reporters. Pelley stated publicly that 60 Minutes' decades-long success came from its integrity and quality journalism, suggesting the show's integrity is now at risk under new leadership.

cards.headline: FBI kills suspect after hostage situation at California bank
cards.teaser: Ten people were held hostage at a Chase Bank in Bakersfield before the suspect was shot dead.
cards.body:
An armed suspect barricaded himself inside a Chase Bank in Bakersfield, California on Tuesday, taking multiple people hostage in a standoff that lasted roughly 12 hours. The suspect, who had a bomb strapped to his body, was shot and killed by the FBI early Wednesday morning.

Two hostages were released on Tuesday, with the remaining hostages freed on Wednesday. Police confirmed that all hostages were released safely and unharmed. The suspect's identity has not been released.

cards.headline: Trump confirms heated phone call with Netanyahu over Beirut bombing plans
cards.teaser: The president acknowledged cursing at the Israeli leader during the conversation but said they still get along.
cards.body:
President Trump confirmed that he called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "crazy" and cursed at him during a heated phone call over military operations in Lebanon. Trump told Netanyahu not to bomb Beirut, the capital of Lebanon.

Despite the confrontational nature of the exchange, Trump stated that he and Netanyahu maintain a working relationship. The public acknowledgment reveals tension between the US and Israel regarding military decisions in the region.

cards.headline: Israeli strikes kill nine in Lebanon as partial ceasefire shows strain
cards.teaser: Hezbollah fired rockets over the border following the deadly Israeli attacks in Lebanon.
cards.body:
Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon have resulted in nine deaths, prompting a retaliatory rocket attack from Hezbollah across the border. These incidents occurred days after Israel and the Lebanese armed group announced a partial ceasefire arrangement.

The escalation tests the fragility of the recent agreement. While Israel has continued its campaign in southern Lebanon, it has refrained from striking Beirut as part of the ceasefire terms brokered by the US. The exchange of fire between the two sides demonstrates that hostilities have not fully ceased despite the partial truce.

cards.headline: Justice Department investigating George Santos over betting activity
cards.teaser: The former congressman's lawyers are in talks with the DOJ about suspicious bets placed on Kalshi.
cards.body:
George Santos confirmed that his lawyers are in discussions with the Justice Department regarding an investigation into his betting activities. Federal authorities are examining whether the disgraced former congressman engaged in insider trading through bets he placed on Kalshi, a prediction market platform.

Santos allegedly wagered on the platform about his own attendance at President Trump's State of the Union address in February. The investigation centers on whether he used non-public information to place these bets.

cards.headline: Seven states sue Trump administration over offshore wind farm cancellation deal
cards.teaser: A coalition of states filed suit over a payment of nearly $1 billion to halt an offshore wind project.
cards.body:
Seven states filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration over a deal that paid French company TotalEnergies nearly $1 billion to cancel offshore wind farm projects. New York joined other states including Maine in the legal challenge against the payment arrangement.

The lawsuit targets the administration's decision to use federal funds to end the offshore wind developments. State attorneys general argue the payment violated legal requirements and undermined renewable energy development along the Atlantic coast.

cards.headline: Social Security benefits could face $500 monthly cuts in 2032, analysis finds
cards.teaser: A new report projects significant reductions to Social Security checks if the trust fund becomes insolvent.
cards.body:
Social Security recipients could see monthly benefits reduced by an average of $500 in 2032 if the program's trust fund runs out of money, according to analysis by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. The projected cuts would affect retirees across all states.

Current projections show the trust fund depleting within six years, which would trigger automatic benefit reductions under existing law unless Congress acts to shore up the program's finances.

cards.headline: Stock markets decline as S&P 500 nine-day winning streak ends
cards.teaser: Major indexes fell as markets pulled back from recent record highs.
cards.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell over 350 points while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 also declined, halting the S&P 500's nine-day winning streak. Markets responded to new employment data from ADP and manufacturing reports from the ISM during the trading session.

The broader pullback followed record highs reached in previous sessions, as investors reassessed their positions after the extended rally. Technology stocks experienced the steepest declines, though some AI and data center companies bucked the trend and posted gains.

cards.headline: European Union announces plan to reduce reliance on American technology
cards.teaser: The 27-nation bloc outlined proposals to expand its own tech infrastructure.
cards.body:
The European Union released a plan to decrease its dependence on American technology companies by expanding the region's capabilities in data centers, semiconductors, and cloud computing. The initiative aims to build up Europe's domestic tech infrastructure across all 27 member nations.

The announcement reflects growing concerns in Europe about technological sovereignty and supply chain security. EU officials outlined how the bloc intends to develop its own capacity in critical technology sectors currently dominated by American firms.

cards.headline: Marvell stock climbs after Nvidia CEO comments on company's potential
cards.teaser: Shares surged following remarks from Jensen Huang about the chipmaker's future.
cards.body:
Marvell Technology's stock price rose toward a record high after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made comments suggesting the company could reach trillion-dollar valuation status. The market added approximately $40 billion to Marvell's market capitalization before midday trading.

The chipmaker has benefited from growing demand for AI data center infrastructure. Analysts pointed to the company's positioning in the artificial intelligence supply chain as a key catalyst for the stock's recent performance and future growth prospects.

cards.headline: CBS News editor Bari Weiss addresses Scott Pelley firing
cards.teaser: The editor in chief spoke publicly about the dismissal of the longtime correspondent.
cards.body:
CBS News editor in chief Bari Weiss commented on the firing of Scott Pelley, saying the longtime 60 Minutes correspondent broke trust within the newsroom. Weiss made her first public remarks about the dismissal, stating Pelley chose a particular path that led to his departure.

The firing followed a heated staff meeting where Pelley confronted CBS News management over recent personnel changes. He had objected to the network's decision to remove the show's executive producer, executive editor, and correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as part of a broader overhaul of 60 Minutes.

hero.headline: NASA ends recovery efforts for MAVEN Mars orbiter after six months of silence
hero.body:
NASA has officially declared its MAVEN spacecraft lost after six months without contact. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution orbiter, which has studied Mars since 2014, abruptly stopped communicating with ground stations in early December 2025. After exhausting recovery attempts, the agency announced the end of the mission.

MAVEN launched in 2013 and arrived at Mars the following year to study the planet's upper atmosphere and understand how Mars lost most of its air over billions of years. The spacecraft made groundbreaking discoveries about atmospheric loss processes and detected auroras in the Martian sky, similar to Earth's northern lights. The mission helped scientists determine that solar wind stripped away the Martian atmosphere, transforming the planet from a potentially habitable world with liquid water on its surface to the cold, dry desert seen today.

According to NASA's statement, telemetry showed all subsystems working normally before the spacecraft orbited behind Mars. When it reappeared, there was only silence. The spacecraft and operations teams investigated the anomaly to try to address the situation, but ultimately could not restore communication.

The orbiter operated well beyond its original mission timeline, collecting data about Mars' atmospheric escape, solar wind interactions, and magnetic field remnants. MAVEN provided observations during multiple Martian years and served as a crucial communication relay for NASA's two Mars rovers, Curiosity and Perseverance. The spacecraft also monitored space weather conditions around Mars, tracking solar storms and their effects on the thin Martian atmosphere.

NASA attempted various recovery procedures over the six-month period, including sending commands through the Deep Space Network and adjusting communication protocols. Engineers explored multiple scenarios that could have caused the communication failure, ranging from spacecraft orientation issues to power system problems. The agency maintained hope throughout the recovery period but ultimately determined the spacecraft could not be restored to operational status.

The loss of MAVEN reduces NASA's ability to monitor Martian atmospheric conditions and eliminates a key relay station for surface missions. However, the mission achieved its primary science objectives and generated a comprehensive dataset about Mars' atmosphere that researchers will continue analyzing for years to come.

NASA operates other spacecraft around Mars that remain active. The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, launched in 2005, and Mars Odyssey, launched in 2001, continue their missions and can partially fill some of the observational gaps left by MAVEN's silence. These remaining orbiters will help maintain NASA's presence around the red planet and continue supporting surface exploration efforts.

cards.headline: Hackers accessed customer health data from Ultrahuman through infected employee laptop
cards.teaser: The wearable ring maker disclosed a security breach after attackers obtained credentials from malware on an employee device.
cards.body:
Ultrahuman, which makes wearable rings for tracking health metrics, confirmed that hackers accessed customer wellness data through an internal tool. The breach began when attackers infected an employee's laptop with malware and stole the credentials stored on it.

Using the stolen credentials, the hackers gained unauthorized access to an internal system that contained customer information collected by Ultrahuman's devices, including sleep patterns and activity levels.

cards.headline: Sun produces three major solar flares in 24 hours, raising chances for aurora displays
cards.teaser: A series of powerful eruptions from the sun increased the likelihood of northern lights visible at lower latitudes.
cards.body:
The sun released three colossal solar flares in less than 24 hours, including the highest X-class flare recorded during the current solar cycle. NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory detected the eruptions, which sent plasma streams toward Earth and triggered a brief S1-level solar radiation storm.

The flares originated from different regions on the sun's surface, including the far side and the geoeffective Region 4455. Space weather forecasters indicated the solar activity would boost opportunities for aurora displays at northern latitudes as charged particles interact with Earth's magnetic field.

cards.headline: Instagram notifies users targeted in AI chatbot hacking attacks
cards.teaser: Meta began alerting victims after hackers exploited a support chatbot to gain account access even after a reported fix.
cards.body:
Instagram has begun notifying users who were targeted by hackers exploiting vulnerabilities in its AI-powered support chatbot. The attackers used the automated system to gain unauthorized access to victim accounts.

The breach persisted even after Meta announced it had patched the chatbot security flaw. Some reports have connected the incidents to recent high-profile account hijackings on the platform.

cards.headline: AI music startup Suno raises $400 million while facing copyright litigation
cards.teaser: The music generation company reached a valuation above $5.4 billion despite ongoing legal challenges from rights holders.
cards.body:
Suno has raised $400 million in new funding, pushing its valuation to over $5.4 billion—more than double its $2.45 billion valuation from seven months prior.

The AI music-generation startup continues to defend itself against copyright lawsuits while expanding its operations. The platform enables users to create original music through text prompts, though rights holders have disputed whether the company obtained proper permissions for the data used to train its system.

cards.headline: Apple scales back Vision product plans, shifts focus to smart glasses
cards.teaser: CEO John Ternus reduced the Vision headset roadmap as the company redirects resources toward glasses development.
cards.body:
Apple narrowed its plans for Vision Pro successor products under CEO John Ternus. Analyst reports indicate the company took Vision Pro follow-up devices off the development schedule and redirected efforts toward smart glasses instead.

Apple aims to disrupt the eyewear market similarly to its Apple Watch entry into wearables. Smart glasses projects have been delayed until 2027 or later, with AI-enabled glasses still scheduled for next year according to some analysts. The shift represents a strategic pivot away from the mixed-reality headset category.

cards.headline: Google releases Fitbit Air design specifications for third-party accessory makers
cards.teaser: The company published CAD drawings and technical guidelines allowing anyone to manufacture bands and accessories for the device.
cards.body:
Google made the complete technical specifications and CAD drawings for the Fitbit Air publicly available. The release enables third-party manufacturers and hobbyists to create custom bands, cases, and other accessories that fit the fitness tracker precisely.

The specifications include detailed measurements and mounting guidelines for accessory development. Google's decision allows users to 3D print their own accessories or purchase from independent makers, including options like bicep bands for different wearing positions beyond the standard wrist mount.

hero.headline: Nick Saban testifies before Congress in support of college sports legislation
hero.body:
Former Alabama head coach Nick Saban appeared before Congress on Wednesday to advocate for the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act, legislation designed to regulate name, image and likeness compensation and transfer portal rules in college athletics. Saban told lawmakers the bill would "bring order to a system that badly needs fixing" in the current era of NIL deals and unrestricted player movement.

The proposed legislation addresses growing concerns about the rapidly changing landscape of college sports since athletes gained the right to profit from their NIL in 2021. The transfer portal, which allows players to switch schools with fewer restrictions, has also transformed college athletics. Coaches, administrators and some athletes have raised concerns that the lack of federal regulation has created an uneven playing field across schools and conferences.

Saban retired from coaching Alabama in January after winning six national championships with the Crimson Tide. During his tenure, he became one of the most successful coaches in college football history. His appearance before Congress reflects his continued involvement in shaping the future of college athletics even after stepping away from coaching. The bipartisan nature of the Protect College Sports Act signals potential momentum for federal legislation in an area that has largely been governed by NCAA rules and individual state laws.

The testimony comes as college sports faces pressure to establish clear rules around athlete compensation and movement between programs. Without federal guidelines, schools in states with more permissive NIL laws may have recruiting advantages over institutions in states with stricter regulations. The transfer portal has also raised questions about roster stability and the student-athlete experience as players increasingly move between programs.

Saban's support for federal intervention adds significant weight to efforts to standardize rules across college athletics. His experience as one of the sport's most successful leaders gives credibility to the argument that the current system requires government regulation.

The Protect College Sports Act represents an attempt by lawmakers to create uniform standards for NIL compensation and transfer rules that would apply to all NCAA member institutions. Congress has explored various approaches to regulating college sports in recent years as the traditional amateur model has given way to a system where athletes can earn substantial income through endorsements and sponsorships while remaining eligible to compete.

Establishing federal standards could help level the competitive landscape across different regions and conferences. Currently, some states have enacted their own NIL laws, creating a patchwork of regulations that puts certain programs at disadvantages compared to others. Federal legislation would eliminate these inconsistencies and provide clarity for schools, athletes and coaches navigating the modern college sports environment. The bill's bipartisan support suggests there may be sufficient congressional backing to move the legislation forward in coming months.

cards.headline: Santa Clara County issues arrest warrant for 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk
cards.teaser: The warrant stems from a misdemeanor charge of exhibition of speeding after a social media post.
cards.body:
The Santa Clara County District Attorney's office has issued an arrest warrant for San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk on a misdemeanor charge of exhibition of speeding, following a viral social media post.

Aiyuk is in his fifth season with the 49ers after being selected in the first round of the 2020 NFL Draft. Last season, he recorded 1,342 receiving yards and seven touchdowns, establishing himself as a key offensive weapon for the team.

cards.headline: Knicks center Mitchell Robinson cleared to play in playoff opener
cards.teaser: Robinson practiced Tuesday and will be available for Game 1 on Wednesday after hand surgery.
cards.body:
New York Knicks center Mitchell Robinson will be available to play in Game 1 on Wednesday after recovering from hand surgery, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Robinson participated in practice on Tuesday, demonstrating sufficient recovery to return to game action.

The return of Robinson provides the Knicks with their starting center for the playoff series. His availability addresses a significant roster concern as New York prepares for the postseason matchup.

cards.headline: Texas and Texas Tech meet in Women's College World Series finals
cards.teaser: The all-Texas championship series begins Wednesday in Oklahoma City.
cards.body:
The Women's College World Series finals begin Wednesday with an in-state showdown between Texas and Texas Tech. Both programs advanced through the tournament bracket to compete for the 2026 national championship in softball.

Texas softball player Hannah Wells has embraced a dugout good luck tradition during the tournament, which has proven effective as she collected four hits in Monday's game.

cards.headline: Former Browns coordinator Jim Schwartz explains resignation after being passed over for head coach
cards.teaser: Schwartz stepped down in February after Cleveland hired a different candidate for the top job.
cards.body:
Jim Schwartz resigned from his position as Cleveland Browns defensive coordinator in February after being passed over for the head coaching job. Schwartz explained his decision to step down, stating that forced marriages fail.

Schwartz joined the Browns as defensive coordinator but sought the head coaching position when it became available. Cleveland's decision to hire a different candidate prompted his departure from the organization.

cards.headline: Prosecutors drop charges against Falcons rookie Zachariah Branch
cards.teaser: Branch was arrested days before the NFL draft on misdemeanor charges that have now been dismissed.
cards.body:
Georgia state prosecutors have dismissed two misdemeanor charges against Atlanta Falcons rookie wide receiver Zachariah Branch. The charges stemmed from an arrest that took place days before the NFL draft, according to his attorney.

Branch was selected by Atlanta in the draft and is now beginning his professional career with the team with the legal matter resolved.

cards.headline: PGA Tour considers two-tier tournament structure for 2028
cards.teaser: The proposed model would create separate tracks with promotion and relegation between levels.
cards.body:
A proposed future PGA Tour model that might take effect in 2028 would include two tracks of tournaments with players competing to remain on the top track and golfers in the lower track fighting to move up the next season. The structure would create a tiered system within professional golf.

The model represents a significant departure from the current PGA Tour format. Players would face annual evaluation based on their performance, with movement between the two tracks determined by results throughout the season.

hero.headline: CBS fires correspondent Scott Pelley as 60 Minutes faces staff upheaval
hero.body:
CBS News fired veteran correspondent Scott Pelley on Tuesday following a heated confrontation with network leadership over the show's direction. The dismissal came days after the network terminated the show's executive producer, executive editor, and two other correspondents, Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega.

The conflict escalated during a staff meeting on Monday when Pelley directly criticized Bari Weiss, the network's editor-in-chief. "She's murdering 60 Minutes," Pelley said, according to sources. "She does not love this place. She was brought in to kill it and is doing exactly that." When CBS News managing editor Charles Forelle called Pelley's remarks rude, Pelley pointed to how the network had treated Tanya Simon, the fired executive producer.

The staff responded with a standing ovation for Pelley, signaling strong internal support for the correspondent. However, newly appointed executive producer Nick Bilton told Pelley he would not be intimidated by his remarks.

After his firing, Pelley issued a public statement accusing network executives of pressuring him to compromise journalistic standards. He claimed they instructed him "to inject falsehoods and bias" into reporting and gave politicians inappropriate input into interviews. Pelley emphasized that the show's decades-long success stemmed from its reputation for "integrity, quality, and humanity."

The departures of Alfonsi and Vega preceded Pelley's confrontation. Alfonsi released a statement saying the boundary between editorial independence and corporate interests was being dismantled. She noted that journalists willing to challenge authority were being sidelined. Vega similarly alleged that teams experienced pressure to insert political bias and that reporters held back story pitches out of fear of internal repercussions, calling the situation "censorship."

At the News and Documentary Emmy awards, held after Alfonsi's departure was announced, Pelley publicly praised her and an 18-year-old high school student who criticized the network's direction under Weiss. Alfonsi had previously reported a segment about a Salvadoran prison that Weiss shelved.

Bari Weiss defended the firings by telling outlets that Pelley violated "trust and mutual respect," though specifics were not detailed. She stated the personnel moves reflected decisions Pelley chose to make.

The rapid succession of departures has raised significant concerns throughout the media industry about the future of the storied newsmagazine. Analysts have characterized the situation as an existential crisis for a program that has been a cornerstone of American broadcast journalism since 1968. The upheaval represents a pivotal moment for CBS News as it grapples with questions about editorial independence and the show's ability to maintain its prestigious reputation.

cards.headline: Netflix releases Michael Jackson documentary examining singer and public perception
cards.teaser: The streaming service launched a docuseries that revisits allegations and legal battles that followed the late entertainer.
cards.body:
Netflix released Michael Jackson: The Verdict, a docuseries examining the late singer and public perception of his legacy. The series revisits Jackson's legal battles and the accusations of misconduct that followed him throughout his life and after his death nearly two decades ago.

The documentary explores the contrast between Jackson's status as a singular entertainer with timeless music and the serious allegations that have shaped his public image. The series frames its examination as putting both the singer and the public on trial.

cards.headline: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey to screen in 70mm at Los Angeles theater
cards.teaser: The film will run for three weeks at Westwood's Village Theatre starting in July.
cards.body:
Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey will have a special three-week theatrical run beginning July 17 at the Village Theatre in Westwood. The American Cinematheque is partnering with Universal Pictures and the Village Directors Circle to present the film in 70mm format, with three showtimes offered daily.

Tickets go on sale Thursday at 9 a.m. The 70mm format delivers enhanced image detail and clarity compared to standard digital projection, a large-format approach Nolan has consistently favored throughout his filmmaking career.

cards.headline: Sara Bareilles announces first album in seven years and fall tour
cards.teaser: The singer will release Good Grief on Aug. 28 and tour North American theaters in September and October.
cards.body:
Sara Bareilles will release her first studio album in seven years on Aug. 28. The album, titled Good Grief, will be followed by a tour of North American theaters in September and October.

Bareilles has maintained a low profile as a performing and recording artist since before the pandemic. The new album and tour mark her return to active recording and concert work after an extended break from those activities.

cards.headline: Casting Society adds video game casting as membership category
cards.teaser: Professionals in senior game casting roles can now apply for membership in the organization.
cards.body:
The Casting Society has added video game casting as a membership qualification category. The change allows professionals who work in game casting to apply for membership in the organization, which previously recognized primarily film and television work.

The new category applies to those who have worked in senior or principal casting roles within the video game industry. Eligible positions include casting directors and senior casting personnel who have handled game projects.

cards.headline: Sharon Stone discusses Marc Maron's performance in In Memoriam
cards.teaser: The actress talked about helping the comedian tackle an emotional scene in the new film.
cards.body:
Sharon Stone spoke about working with Marc Maron on In Memoriam, a film in which the comedian and podcaster plays an actor. Maron expressed concerns about his ability to perform a key emotional scene that required him to cry, questioning whether he had sufficient control as an actor.

The film gave Maron an opportunity to channel grief over the death of filmmaker Lynn Shelton. Stone also commented on a proposed Basic Instinct reboot by screenwriter Joe Eszterhas, calling it a bad idea.

cards.headline: Weezer previews self-titled album with new single featuring Wednesday
cards.teaser: The band released We Might As Well Be Strangers ahead of the album's August release.
cards.body:
Weezer has shared a new single called "We Might As Well Be Strangers" featuring the artist Wednesday. The track serves as a preview of the band's upcoming self-titled album, arriving August 21.

The album includes the previously released single "Shine Again." This marks another self-titled release from the veteran rock band, which has returned to that naming convention multiple times throughout its career.

hero.headline: Pentagon inspector general to oversee Iran war investigation
hero.body:
The Pentagon's top watchdog has been designated to lead an investigation into the U.S. military operations against Iran, according to an announcement from the Defense Department's Office of Inspector General. Cheryl L. Mason, chair of the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency, named Pentagon Inspector General Platte B. Moring III as the lead inspector for the probe.

The appointment formalizes independent oversight of the military campaign. Inspector general investigations typically examine how military operations are conducted, whether they comply with legal authorities, and how federal funds are spent. Moring will coordinate the investigation across multiple government agencies involved in the conflict.

The announcement comes as Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been testifying before Congress about the ongoing situation in the Middle East. Rubio appeared before the House, where Democratic lawmakers questioned him about the Iran war and negotiations that have apparently stalled. He was also scheduled to testify before the Senate Appropriations Committee regarding the State Department's fiscal 2027 budget request and the Middle East situation.

The inspector general system functions as an independent check on federal agencies and military operations. When major overseas military operations involve multiple agencies, the government appoints a lead inspector general to provide coordinated oversight and ensure transparency and accountability across departments.

The investigation into Iran war operations will likely examine several key areas. Inspectors are expected to review the legal justification for military action, evaluate the decisions made by military commanders, and assess how funds related to the conflict have been spent. Inspector general reports are typically submitted to Congress and can lead to recommendations for policy changes or measures to hold officials accountable for their actions.

This formal oversight mechanism reflects the government's effort to ensure that major military operations receive independent review. The inspector general system has been used for significant overseas military campaigns to provide Congress and the public with transparent information about how operations are being conducted and resources are being used.

The designation of Moring as lead inspector signals that the investigation will be comprehensive in scope. By coordinating across multiple agencies, the inspector general can examine all aspects of the military campaign, from initial decisions to authorize military action through ongoing operations and spending.

The timing of the investigation, coming as Rubio testified about stalled negotiations and the State Department's budget needs, suggests that questions about the Iran conflict remain significant on Capitol Hill. Congressional Democrats have indicated they want answers about how the military campaign has been conducted and whether diplomatic efforts have been adequately pursued.

cards.headline: Adults with cancer or HIV may lose Medicaid under new work requirements
cards.teaser: Advocates warn that people with serious illnesses could lose coverage if they cannot prove they are too sick to meet the 80-hour monthly work rule.
cards.body:
Adults on Medicaid will be required to work 80 hours per month under new Trump administration work rules. The administration says people who are sick can be exempt if they prove they are too ill to work.

Advocates worry that people with cancer or HIV could lose coverage under these requirements. The concern centers on the burden of documenting serious medical conditions and maintaining exemptions over time.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: The former Interior Secretary could become the first female Native American governor if elected in November.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland, who served as Interior Secretary in the Biden administration, won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico. The victory sets up a general election campaign this November.

If Haaland wins, she would become the first female Native American governor in U.S. history. She previously represented New Mexico in Congress before joining the Biden cabinet.

cards.headline: Hilton and Becerra lead in California governor primary
cards.teaser: Republican Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra are ahead in early returns as California votes to replace outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
Republican Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra are leading in California's gubernatorial primary, with results still being tallied. Hilton held a narrow lead at 28%, followed closely by Becerra. Democrat Tom Steyer also emerged near the top of the crowded field early on.

Under California's top-two primary system, the two candidates with the most votes advance to the general election. With Governor Gavin Newsom leaving office, the race is wide open. A Democrat is expected to win the governorship in the deep-blue state, though the party faces a choice between establishment-backed candidates and more progressive alternatives.

cards.headline: IBM CEO supports Trump AI executive order with minimal regulation
cards.teaser: Arvind Krishna said he prefers light government guardrails over active intervention in artificial intelligence development.
cards.body:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna endorsed the Trump administration's executive order on artificial intelligence and cybersecurity at a summit this week. Krishna expressed support for a light regulatory approach, arguing that excessive government oversight could create bureaucracy that slows technological innovation.

The executive order represents a significant policy shift. Hours before signing, Trump reversed course on a provision that would have required government safety reviews of new AI models before release. The president cited American competitiveness and competition with China as reasons for the lighter regulatory stance, rejecting growing calls from experts and the public for stronger AI safety oversight.

cards.headline: Homeland Security secretary may pull customs agents from sanctuary city airports
cards.teaser: Secretary Mullin said he will keep agents at New Jersey airports as long as state and federal leaders continue cooperating.
cards.body:
Homeland Security Secretary Mullin said he is considering removing customs agents from airports in sanctuary cities. He testified that he will not remove agents from New Jersey airports as long as cooperation between state and federal officials continues.

The statement suggests the administration may use customs enforcement as leverage in disputes with states over immigration policy. Sanctuary cities limit their cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, a policy the Trump administration has opposed.

cards.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent describes confrontation with intelligence nominee Pulte
cards.teaser: Bessent told senators he once told Bill Pulte he was going to kick his rear end.
cards.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testified before the Senate on Wednesday about a past confrontation with Bill Pulte, the Federal Housing Finance Agency Director. Bessent said he once told Pulte that he was going to kick his rear end, though he did not elaborate on what sparked their disagreement.

Pulte was recently selected by President Trump to serve as acting head of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. His nomination has drawn scrutiny, with some Republican senators questioning whether he meets the eligibility requirements for the role.
